answer:
Tracing is the base layer: it records what your application does. Calls "provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation" [S6]. Evaluations measure quality against repeatable test cases [S3]. Signals score your agent's turns in production and point you to the traces that need attention [S1][S7].

**Tracing: capturing what happened**
- Weave's tracing is built on Ops, Calls, Traces, and Threads [S2]. Each time an Op runs, Weave records a Call with its inputs, output, timing, parent/child links, and any errors [S6].
- A Trace is the full tree of Calls that share one execution context [S4].

**Evaluations: structured testing**
- An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call is one evaluation run [S3].
- The goal is to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and catch regressions (cases where a change makes things worse) [S3].

**Signals: monitoring agents in production**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals flag quality and safety issues, such as user frustration or NSFW content, and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- To start scoring your agent's turns, you create signals. A turn is one exchange between the user and the agent [S5][S7].
- **Tags** apply labels such as `user-frustration` to matching spans. **Ratings** give matching spans a score from 0 to 1 so you can measure improvement over time [S7].

**How they fit together**
This is my interpretation of the cited pages. Tracing records the data that the other two build on [S6]. Evaluations score your application on curated, repeatable examples so you can compare versions [S3]. Signals score real agent conversations in production [S1][S7]. In practice: trace your app, use evaluations to measure changes, and use Signals to watch live behavior.

Tracing is the base layer: it records what your application does. Evaluations use that kind of recorded execution to measure quality against fixed test cases. Signals score the conversations of live agents so you can find problem traces in production.

**Tracing: capturing what happened**

- A Trace is the full tree of Calls that share one execution context [S4]. Calls "provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation" [S6].

**Evaluations: testing before release**
- An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call is one evaluation run [S3].
- The goal is to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and catch regressions (cases where a change makes things worse) [S3].

**Signals: monitoring agents in production**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals flag quality and safety issues, such as user frustration or NSFW content, and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- A rating is a score from 0.0 to 1.0, and a tag is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are attached to matching spans [S5].

**How they fit together**
This is my reading of the pages, not a single statement in the docs. Tracing records the data. Evaluations score that kind of behavior offline, on curated examples you control. Signals score live agent traffic, either one turn (one user-agent exchange) at a time or a whole conversation [S1][S5]. Together they give you a loop: trace, evaluate before you ship, then watch production with Signals.

sources.heading: Calls
sources.text:
## Calls

A **Call** is a logged execution of an Op. Every time an Op runs, Weave creates a Call that captures:

* Input arguments
* Output value
* Timing and latency
* Parent-child relationships (for nested calls)
* Any errors that occur

Calls show up as **Traces** in the Weights & Biases UI and provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation. For the full Call object structure and properties, see the [Call schema reference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/call-schema-reference.md).

Calls are similar to spans in the [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) data model. A Call can:

* Belong to a Trace, a collection of Calls in the same execution context.
* Have parent and child Calls, forming a tree structure.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. > [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

all_read_evidence.text:
## Calls

A **Call** is a logged execution of an Op. Every time an Op runs, Weave creates a Call that captures:

* Input arguments
* Output value
* Timing and latency
* Parent-child relationships (for nested calls)
* Any errors that occur

Calls show up as **Traces** in the Weights & Biases UI and provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation. For the full Call object structure and properties, see the [Call schema reference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/call-schema-reference.md).

Calls are similar to spans in the [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) data model. A Call can:

* Belong to a Trace, a collection of Calls in the same execution context.
* Have parent and child Calls, forming a tree structure.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

result.text:
## Calls

A **Call** is a logged execution of an Op. Every time an Op runs, Weave creates a Call that captures:

* Input arguments
* Output value
* Timing and latency
* Parent-child relationships (for nested calls)
* Any errors that occur

Calls show up as **Traces** in the Weights & Biases UI and provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation. For the full Call object structure and properties, see the [Call schema reference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/call-schema-reference.md).

Calls are similar to spans in the [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) data model. A Call can:

* Belong to a Trace, a collection of Calls in the same execution context.
* Have parent and child Calls, forming a tree structure.

result.text:
## Create a new signal

To start scoring your agent's turns, create one or more signals. Select **+ New signal** to open the **Create signals** drawer.

The drawer groups available signals into two categories:

* **Tags**: Apply a label automatically to matching spans, such as `user-frustration` or `nsfw`. Use tags to categorize spans or flag unwanted behavior. The signals UI only displays rows for spans that matched at least one tag, so a tag signal might run successfully even if you don't see any output.
* **Ratings**: Assign a score from 0 to 1 to matching spans. Use ratings to rate agent performance and measure improvements over time.

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

Tracing is the base layer: it records what your application does. Evaluations use that kind of recorded execution to measure quality against fixed test cases. Signals score your agent's turns in production so you can find problem traces.

**Tracing: capturing what happened**
- Weave's tracing is built on Ops, Calls, Traces, and Threads [S2]. Each time an Op runs, Weave records a Call with its inputs, output, timing, parent/child links, and any errors [S6].
- A Trace is the full tree of Calls that share one execution context [S4]. Calls "provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation" [S6].

**Evaluations: testing before release**
- An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call is one evaluation run [S3].
- The goal is to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and catch regressions (cases where a change makes things worse) [S3].

**Signals: monitoring agents in production**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals flag quality and safety issues, such as user frustration or NSFW content, and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- To start scoring your agent's turns, you create signals. A turn is one exchange between the user and the agent [S5][S7].
- **Tags** apply labels such as `user-frustration` to matching spans. **Ratings** give matching spans a score from 0 to 1 so you can measure improvement over time [S7].

**How they fit together**
This is my reading of the pages, not a single statement in the docs. Tracing records the data. Evaluations score behavior offline, on curated examples you control. Signals score live agent turns and show you which traces need attention [S1][S7]. Together they give you a loop: trace, evaluate before you ship, then watch production with Signals.
